name: The Tuttle household — a documented grocer, unplaced in the town
head: tuttle_j_b

arrival.note: A BOUND FROM THE PAPER, NOT AN ARRIVAL. The corpus first prints this person at the Democrat of 4 June 1834, column 11, so they are in the town's paper by 1834-06-04 and at no stated time before it; nothing reached says when they came. Last printed 1834-07-02.

arrival_year.note: DRAWN, NOT READ. The household's arrival block holds a BOUND — somebody was here by 1834-06-04 and no source says when they came — so the year is drawn from the arrival years the known layer records, truncated at that bound and renormalised. It says what a household of this bound most likely was, and nothing whatever about this household.

basis.note: data/reconstruction/1835_town_model.json#arrival_and_origin.tables.arrival_year_of_the_known_layer, restricted to years at or before 1834.

replaceable_by.match: a dated source that says which year this household came to Chicago

origin.note: DRAWN FROM A SURVIVORSHIP SAMPLE. No source says where this household came from. The region is drawn from the birthplaces of the seventy Old Settlers who registered an arrival at or before 1835 — a self-selected roll set down forty-four years later that over-represents the men who stayed and prospered, as the town model's own open questions say. It is the only origin distribution this project holds and this value is drawn from it, not measured.

replaceable_by.match: a source that says where this household came from

reason_for_coming.value: A store for the traffic of a town filling up
reason_for_coming.note: ARGUED FROM THIS HOUSEHOLD'S OWN RECORDED TRADE, WHICH IS NOT ITS MOTIVE. The head is recorded as grocer, and this names the documented draw that trade answered in this town in this decade. It does not claim to know why these people came. Which of these draws brought this household is not recorded, and no committed source apportions the town between them.

basis.note: arrival_fill.trade_reasons.a_store_for_the_traffic — the head's recorded trade is evidence about this household, and the draw it answered is the reason the record will carry until a source states one.

replaceable_by.match: a source that says why this household came, or a committed source that apportions the town's arrivals between the land sales, the canal and the harbour works

lives_at.note: Not attested. NOTHING IS BEING WITHHELD HERE: no source reached says where this person lived, and 52 households in this dataset were already in that position before this one was written.

works_at.note: Not attested as a structure this project models. The trade is documented; the premises are not one of the committed records.

present_on_scene_date.note: THE CORPUS STOPS BEFORE THE SCENE DATE. Last printed 1834-07-02, at the Democrat of 2 July 1834, column 21, and nothing reached either follows this person to 1 July 1835 or says they left. A documented resident whose whereabouts on one day are unknown is `uncertain` here rather than dropped: that is the same distinction index.json draws for Jeremiah Porter, and it is a finding rather than a gap.

persons.name: J. B. Tuttle

occupation.note: THE TRADE IS THE PAPER'S. The corpus reads it as grocer, at the Democrat of 4 June 1834, column 11; the Democrat of 25 June 1834, column 6; the Democrat of 2 July 1834, column 21. The residents vocabulary's nearest period-correct word for it is `grocer`, and where the corpus prints more than one trade they are all named here rather than reduced to the one the vocabulary could take.

persons.note: A DOCUMENTED PERSON, AND NOTHING ELSE IS CLAIMED. The papers name '4. B. TUTTLE' and 'J. B. TUTTL' and 'J. B. TUTTLE' and give the trade; they do not say where this household lived, who else was in it, or when it came. So the record around this person carries nothing but the person: no dwelling, no division, no family, each written as unattested in its own block rather than filled in from the shape of the rest of the town. Cited at the Democrat of 4 June 1834, column 11; the Democrat of 25 June 1834, column 6; the Democrat of 2 July 1834, column 21. The corpus associates the name with Dearborn Street; that is where the paper does business with this person and not a statement about where they slept, and the storefront tickets are the ones that may stand a shop there. THE TOWN NEVER INVENTED A ROOF FOR THIS TRADE. The occupation census raised reconstructed households for the trades a town of 3,265 people needed and could not document; `grocer` was not one of them, which is why this person could only ever be ADDED and never seated on an existing record — data/research/newspapers/register_1835.json calls it `new_resident` for exactly that reason. No figure is drawn (docs/LIBERTIES.md L1). READ THROUGH A TRANSCRIPTION, not a scan: the owner's ruling of 2026-08-28 grades a transcription-mediated reading as documented, and the source record for the run states that standard and its limits. A scan read that confirms or corrects the name upgrades this entry. THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 1 time: Election returns — poll list of 1834, filed 11 August 1834 — “Tuttle, James B.” (poll_1834_109, line 278). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Tuttle' agrees with the entry's forenames; 1 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (data/research/civic/voter_crosswalk.json).

roles.note: THE BOUND IS THE SOURCE'S, NOT THE MAN'S. This role is carried by the card's 1835 occupation block and is dated by what the cited source or sources are ABOUT, which is why `precision` can be no better than the span they cover. The span reaches 1835, so this role stands in the scene-date view. The printing the trade was read off is not on the card and is fetched by T-1254.

research_note: MINTED FROM THE NEWSPAPER REGISTER (T-0376), AND THE HOUSEHOLD IS A CONTAINER RATHER THAN AN ARGUMENT. Every other record in this dataset argues for a household — a family the sources count, or a trade the town demonstrably needed. This one argues for a PERSON: the Democrat and the American name J. B. Tuttle as a grocer at Chicago 3 time(s), and this reconstruction did not hold them. `data/residents/` has no way to carry a person except inside a household, so one was written around them and told to claim nothing: one member, no dwelling, no division, no origin, no arrival beyond the bound the paper sets. Reading a family, a house or a quarter of town into this record would be reading something the papers do not say. tools/mint_documented_residents.py derives the whole minted set and prints every candidate it refused, with the reason.
